name: Fallen leaf
lede: Fallen leaf is a dull gold-brown that our library also carries, at the identical hex, from a Japanese traditional color list.

sections.title: A leaf, twice over
sections.body:
Our library records this name from a Japanese traditional-color source, with no further date given [1]. The same hex appears again under [[light-hazel]], also from a Japanese list, where the source note carries the characters 青朵葉, read literally as a blue-green fallen leaf [1]. The ISCC-NBS system reads the swatch as a light yellow, about 3.7 units from the block center [1].

The nearest other named colors are [[pinchbeck-brown]] and [[honey-yellow]], both under 6 units away [2]. The family is [[leaf]], a plant word rather than a mineral or animal one [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This color, as photographed, appears in 1,232 of 23,781 paintings, about 5.18 percent, more common than 89 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 49 of 945 paintings, at 5.2 percent of that period's paintings, 1.3 times the overall rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent [3]. Its most devoted painter is Fritz Thomsen, carrying it in 6 of 18 works here, 6.9 times the baseline for his museums [3]. The earliest match in the archive is a 1240 painting by Master of the Cross 434; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first, and no date is implied for the name itself [3].

issues: Fixed: the field-notes paragraph (and the matching "field" object) invented a country claim ("over-represented in Iranian painting, 8 of 29") with no basis — ar.co is empty for this slug (the real over-representation is a movement, Mughal, 13 of 168, 2.9x, which went unmentioned) — and an earliest-match claim ("a Roman carved fragment from about 1 CE") that doesn't match the real first-seen record (a 1240 painting by Master of the Cross 434). The presence count (1,062) also didn't match either real count (898 within-painting / 1,232 as-photographed). The Paulus Potter painter stat was accurate but wasn't this slug's most-devoted painter (Fritz Thomsen, 6 of 18, is). Rewrote the paragraph directly from data/graph/fieldnotes for this slug; removed every unsupported claim rather than inventing a replacement for it.
